seo.title: About
seo.description: Navin Bhattarai's story: from his grandfather's screwdriver in Gaindakot, Nepal, to physics at Truman State, mechanical engineering at WashU, teaching, and a PhD in Fall 2027.

header.title: The longer story.
body: I'm a mechanical engineer and thermal-fluids researcher from Gaindakot, a small town on the Narayani River in Nepal. I'm finishing a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering at WashU this December, after a B.A. in Physics at Truman State.
I build CFD simulations and topology optimization for battery cold plates, and I distrust my own results until they earn it. I'm applying to PhD programs for Fall 2027.
header.imageAlt: Portrait of Navin smiling, in a white T-shirt, in a library

tools.title: Pick a tool, get a story.
tools.sub: Every one of these has been in my hands for a reason.

list.label: Screwdriver
list.title: “Kancha, pass me that screwdriver.”
body: My grandfather was my first mentor. He was a farmer with a vintage Massey Ferguson 35 tractor (older than my father), and he fixed old gadgets and took care of the things around the house that everyone else ignored.
During Tihar in 2013, he was hanging Jhilimili lights and called out for a screwdriver. The next year, I wired the lights myself, while my grandmother told me to stay away from the electricity.
He never went to college, but he's an engineer in my eyes. I got my habit from him: I can't unsee a thing that needs attention. I'll spend 30 minutes now so someone isn't annoyed for a year.

list.label: Wrench
list.title: Dad's engine-parts shop
body: My father runs an automobile and engine-parts business: tractor parts, engine components, piston rings. I spent hours among the new replacement parts and the greasy, broken ones from the repair shop.

I remember staring at a massive tractor engine opened into two halves, its hollow cavities slick with oil, trying to imagine how it worked. I read the car magazines he brought home instead of storybooks.
I admire how hard he works. I only really understood it after working hard myself in the U.S.

list.label: Pencil
list.title: Feel the sign convention
body: When I teach Statics, I ask students to pull or twist the pencil in their hand to feel which way a force or moment points. Then I connect integrals and derivatives to load, shear and moment diagrams, so the math has something to hold on to.
My line to students: “I can be wrong, let's do this together.” My favorite moment is a student telling me they'd never have understood something without me.

list.label: Mesh
list.title: Learn by doing, then go back for the why
body: I don't always wait to fully understand before I start. I dive in, track every step, retrace to whatever broke, and once it works, I dig into why.
All summer, I saw the Courant number in every OpenFOAM run. Then it showed up in my graduate CFD course, and that moment made me want to learn the rest.
My golden key: always remember how you reached each step, so you can step back and redo the wrong one. Either I know it, or I'll make myself learn it.

teaching.title: The thing I enjoy most, besides research
body: I'm an Undergraduate Teaching Fellow at WashU's McKelvey School of Engineering (since Aug 2025). I support Statics, Mechanics of Materials, Solid Mechanics and Thermodynamics, with 80–150 students per course, hold weekly office hours, and led J-Term sessions in Statics and Mechanics of Materials for about 15 students.
Before that, I was an Academic Peer Tutor at Truman State (2023–2025) for Calculus I–III and Physics I–II, including in-class embedded tutoring.
My style is real-life examples and simple breakdowns. And if a student's grade suddenly drops, my first question is “Are you okay?”

headed.title: Simulations I can trust, for energy systems.
headed.quote: The questions I care about now go past what I can teach myself. I can debug a setup until it runs; what I want is the training to know whether it is right, and the judgment to pick problems worth the effort.
body: Next, I want to put heat into the optimizer's objective so designs reach the whole plate; understand when branching, leaf-vein-like channel networks emerge from optimization, and whether they hold up in 3D and in a real flow loop; and check simulations against experiments.

Ten years from now, I hope to lead a lab that builds trustworthy simulation and optimization tools for thermal-fluid energy systems, with industry partners close enough that results reach real engines and batteries, and with teaching at its center. My larger hope: to bring better energy technology to communities like the one I grew up in.

outside.title: A few more things about me
outside.imageAlt: Navin on a boat, fist raised and smiling, with the Statue of Liberty behind him
facts: I earned college credit, with an A, for a class on Dungeons & Dragons. I also took Italian Film.
I trekked to Upper Mustang in the Himalayas with friends. When the altitude got hard, I pushed the group to stay together.
I like trying new sports and can usually hold my own the first time: tennis, indoor simulator golf, cricket (Truman Cricket Club), soccer, basketball.
I once fixed a Camry touchscreen I'd never worked on, by trial, error, some luck, and remembering every step so I could backtrack.
Energy is the thread: a ninth-grade concept for a hydropower dam in my hometown, then solar cells, now battery cold plates.
I'm part of the Nepalese Student Association, the South Asian Student Union and ASME.
